intro: Papis is a hearty beef and tendon stew with baked beans that give its savory broth a gentle sweetness.
ingredients: Freshly ground black pepper, to taste
Cooking oil, enough to coat the bottom of the pot
steps: Heat a thin coating of oil in a heavy pot over medium heat. Cook the garlic and onion, stirring, until fragrant and the onion has softened.
Add the brisket and increase the heat to medium-high. Turn the pieces occasionally until browned on all sides.

Pour in the beef stock and water, then add the tendons. Bring to a boil, lower the heat and maintain a gentle simmer for about 2 hours. Check periodically and replenish water if the pot threatens to dry out; by the end, aim for roughly half the starting liquid and tender beef and tendons.
Stir in the baked beans, sugar and a little salt. Simmer over low heat for another 20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the beans are heated through and the broth has thickened slightly.
Taste the stew and adjust the salt and freshly ground black pepper before serving hot.

intro: Fried Galunggong with Salted Egg and Tomato Salad pairs crisp, simply seasoned fish with a juicy tomato salad enriched by salted egg.
steps: Coat the fish with the salt, working some into each cavity. Leave for 15 minutes.
While the fish rests, gently mix the salted egg, tomato, scallion and fish sauce in a bowl. Set the salad aside.

Heat the oil in a wide frying pan over medium-high heat until shimmering. Carefully lower the fish into the oil, leaving space between them; cook in batches if necessary. Use a splatter screen if available.

Fry the first side until browned and crisp, approximately 5–7 minutes depending on the size of the fish. The vigorous crackling should become quieter as the surface crisps. Turn carefully and fry the other side until equally crisp and the flesh is opaque and separates easily from the bone.
Lift the fish out and allow excess oil to drain. Serve immediately with the salted egg and tomato salad and spicy vinegar.

intro: Adobong kamaru is a crisp, tangy Pampanga pulutan where cleaned mole crickets are cooked with vinegar, aromatics, tomato, and chili.
steps: Rinse the prepared kamaru quickly and drain very well so they fry instead of steam.
Heat oil over medium heat; saute garlic and onion for 2 minutes, then add tomatoes and chilies until softened.
Add kamaru and cook over medium-high heat for 5 to 7 minutes, stirring, until lightly toasted.
Pour in vinegar, season with salt and pepper, and simmer uncovered for 8 to 10 minutes until sharp but not watery.
Cook a few minutes longer until nearly dry and glossy; serve hot with calamansi wedges.

intro: A creamy, fruity Filipino freezer treat that turns shredded melon into refreshing ice candy for hot afternoons.
steps: In a large pitcher or mixing bowl, combine the shredded melon, evaporated milk, water, and sugar.
Stir well until the sugar is fully dissolved and the melon is evenly distributed through the mixture.
Carefully pour the mixture into ice candy plastic bags, leaving enough space to tie each bag securely.
Freeze until completely firm, ideally overnight, then serve straight from the freezer.

intro: Pork belly takes on a smoky, savory-sweet glaze after a calamansi and garlic marinade. Serve with rice and a sharp vinegar dip.
ingredients: 800 g pork belly, sliced about 1 cm thick
Vinegar and chopped chili, to serve
steps: Mix the soy sauce, calamansi juice, garlic, sugar, and pepper. Coat the pork belly and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes.
Lift the pork from the marinade and pat off excess liquid. Brush the slices lightly with oil.
Heat a grill or grill pan to medium. Cook the pork for about 5 to 7 minutes per side, turning as needed, until well browned and cooked through.
Rest the pork for 5 minutes, then slice. Serve with rice and vinegar with chili.

intro: Crispy Pata Sisig turns leftover pork into a fiery, tangy skillet dish with sweet onion and rich chicken liver.
ingredients: 1 lb leftover crispy pata meat, bones removed
steps: Stir the sugar into the vinegar until dissolved. Toss the pork with this mixture and refrigerate for 30 minutes.
Place the pork, its vinegar mixture and the chilies in a food processor. Use short pulses until everything is evenly minced, stopping before it becomes a paste. Scrape into a bowl.
Melt the margarine or butter in a large pan over medium heat. Add the sweet onion and cook, stirring occasionally, until soft. Stir in the chicken liver and cook for 2 minutes.

Add the minced pork and chilies, onion powder, black pepper and salt. Cook over medium heat for 8–10 minutes, stirring frequently, until the mixture is steaming hot throughout and the liver is fully cooked.
Spoon onto a serving plate and serve hot.

intro: Binondo-style tahu goreng pairs crisp fried tofu with cucumber, onion, peanuts, sesame, herbs, and a tangy-sweet soy vinegar sauce.
steps: Heat enough oil for deep-frying in a wok or deep fryer to 180 C.
Drain the tofu thoroughly and pat dry with paper towels, then fry until the outside is golden and crisp; remove and drain.
In a bowl, mix the water, Chinkiang vinegar, soy sauce, kecap manis, and dark brown sugar until the sugar is mostly dissolved.
Heat a little oil in a saucepan over low heat and gently saute the minced garlic until fragrant, then pour in the sauce mixture.
Raise the heat to medium, bring the sauce to a boil, and simmer for 2 minutes until slightly rounded in flavor.
Score the tops of the fried tofu so the sauce can seep in, place on plates, and spoon the hot sauce over them.
Top with cucumber, white onion, peanuts, sesame seeds, coriander, and sambal oelek before serving.

intro: Sotanghon And Egg Noodle Soup brings together slippery glass noodles, tender cabbage and boiled eggs in a warm, garlic-scented broth.
ingredients: 2 teaspoons fish sauce, plus more to taste
steps: Warm the oil in a soup pot over medium heat. Add the crushed garlic and stir until its edges begin to brown, then add the onion and cook until softened.
Mix in the annatto powder and 2 teaspoons of fish sauce. Add the water, raise the heat and bring the broth to a boil.
Add the glass noodles and chicken powder. Cover and allow the broth to boil again, then lower the heat and simmer for 3 minutes.
Use tongs or a spoon to gently separate the noodles. Fold in the shredded cabbage, cover and simmer for another 2 minutes, until the cabbage is just tender and the noodles are pliable.
Add the boiled eggs and green onions and let the eggs warm through. Taste and season with additional fish sauce and ground black pepper as needed.
Divide the noodles, broth and eggs among five bowls. Sprinkle with the toasted garlic and serve hot.

intro: A creamy, spicy vegetable dish with crisp green beans, coconut milk, pork, and chilies. Adjust the heat at the table.
ingredients: 400 g green beans, trimmed and sliced thinly
Salt and black pepper, to taste
steps: Heat oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Cook the onion and garlic until softened and fragrant.
Add the ground pork and break it up with a spoon. Cook until the pork is no longer pink and begins to brown.
Stir in the fish sauce and coconut milk. Simmer gently for 5 minutes, stirring so the coconut milk does not scorch.
Add the green beans and chilies. Cook for 6 to 8 minutes until the beans are tender but still bright. Season with salt and pepper and serve warm.

intro: Pansate is a saucy Filipino-Chinese noodle dish with pork, vegetables, and a glossy soy-oyster gravy finished with calamansi or lemon.
ingredients: Freshly ground black pepper, to taste
Lemon wedges or calamansi, to serve
steps: Soak the fresh yellow noodles in boiling water for 1 minute, then drain, rinse under cold running water, and set aside.
Heat a wok over high heat, add oil, and stir-fry the pork for about 2 minutes until browned; remove the pork and set aside.
Add more oil if the wok looks dry, then saute the shallots and garlic until fragrant; add the carrot and spring onions and stir-fry for 1 minute.
In a bowl, mix the cornstarch, chicken stock, soy sauce, and oyster sauce, then pour into the wok and bring to a boil until the sauce thickens.
Add the noodles and Chinese cabbage and cook over high heat for about 2 minutes, letting the noodles absorb some sauce; add a splash of water only if the pan gets too dry.
Return the pork to the wok, season with fish sauce and freshly ground black pepper, and toss until everything is hot.
Finish with a drizzle of sesame oil and serve with lemon wedges or calamansi.

intro: Light, crisp squid rings with a quick seasoned coating. Fry in small batches so the calamari stays tender.
ingredients: 600 g cleaned squid, cut into rings
steps: Pat the squid rings dry with paper towels. Mix flour, cornstarch, salt, and pepper in a shallow bowl.
Dip the squid in beaten egg, then coat lightly with the flour mixture. Shake off excess coating.
Heat about 5 cm of oil to 175°C in a deep pan. Fry the squid in small batches for 2 to 3 minutes until lightly golden; avoid crowding the pan.
Drain on a rack or paper towels. Serve at once with calamansi wedges and your favorite dip.

intro: This indulgent dish gives tender beef shank a crisp panko crust and a glossy sweet-savory teriyaki sauce.
ingredients: 1/4 cup brown sugar or muscovado sugar
3 tablespoons cold water, for dissolving cornstarch
steps: Place the beef shank and 8 cups water in a pressure cooker and cook under pressure for 15 to 20 minutes, just until tender enough while still holding its shape.
Lift out the beef shank and let it cool slightly, then mix the salt, 1 teaspoon garlic powder, and black pepper and rub the seasoning all over the meat; rest for 10 minutes.
Heat the cooking oil in a deep, wide pot over medium heat. Coat each beef shank in flour, shake off excess, dip in beaten egg, then press into panko until fully covered.
Deep-fry over medium heat for about 10 minutes, turning as needed, until the crumb coating is golden brown and crisp; drain on paper towels.
For the sauce, combine dark soy sauce, ginger powder, 1/4 teaspoon garlic powder, sugar, honey, and 1 cup water in a saucepan and bring to a boil over medium heat.
Stir the cornstarch with 3 tablespoons cold water, pour it into the boiling sauce, and keep stirring until the sauce thickens to a glossy coating consistency.
Serve the fried bulalo hot with the teriyaki sauce on the side or spooned over the top.

intro: A creamy Cavite-style seafood soup loaded with shellfish, fish, and crab in a smooth clam-stock broth.
ingredients: Freshly ground black pepper, to taste
steps: Melt the butter in a pot over low heat, then cook the garlic and onion until fragrant and softened without browning.
Stir in the flour and cook briefly, mixing constantly, until it forms a smooth roux.
Slowly pour in the clam stock while stirring to prevent lumps, then bring the broth to a gentle boil.
Add the shrimp, squid, crab meat, and mussels; return to a gentle boil and simmer for 5 minutes, just until the shellfish begins to cook through.
Add the fish cubes and evaporated milk, lower the heat to a mild simmer, and cook for 8 minutes more, or until the fish is opaque and the soup is creamy.
Season with fish sauce and freshly ground black pepper, then serve hot.

intro: Crisp panko-crusted pork chops make a hearty plate when served alongside savory adobo rice and egg.
steps: Season the pork chops all over with salt and ground black pepper, then let them stand for 15 minutes.
Place the beaten eggs in one bowl and the panko breadcrumbs in another shallow bowl.
Heat the cooking oil in a frying pan; once hot, lower the heat so the coating can brown without burning before the pork cooks through.
Dip each pork chop in beaten egg, then coat completely with panko breadcrumbs, pressing gently so the crumbs adhere.
Pan-fry the pork chops for 6 to 9 minutes per side, adjusting the heat gradually as needed, until the crust is golden and the center is cooked through.
Transfer the crusted pork chops to a serving plate and serve hot with adobo rice and egg if available.

intro: Spicy tokwa't baboy combines tender pig ears, fried tofu, chilies, and a sharp soy-vinegar dressing built for pulutan-style sharing.
ingredients: 3 slices extra firm tofu, 12 oz total
12 to 15 cups water, plus more as needed
steps: Bring 12 to 15 cups water to a boil in a pot, add the pig ears, and boil over medium heat for 15 minutes.
Discard the boiling water, cool the pig ears enough to handle, then scrape them clean to remove hair and the outer skin.
Refill the pot with the same amount of fresh water and bring it to a boil; add the pig ears, lemongrass, and cinnamon bark if using.
Cover and boil over medium heat for about 1 hour, adding more water if needed, until the pig ears are tender.
While the ears cook, heat the cooking oil in a pan and fry the tofu for 4 minutes on one side, then 4 to 5 minutes on the other side, until firm and lightly crisp; drain and cut into cubes.
Remove the cooked pig ears from the pot, let them cool, slice into serving pieces, and combine with the tofu cubes.
Mix the vinegar, soy sauce, sugar, and salt, warm briefly for about 15 seconds, then stir until dissolved.
Add the Thai chilies, long green peppers, red onion, and black pepper to the vinegar mixture, then pour over the tofu and pig ears.
Toss well, top with chopped onion leeks, and serve.

intro: Suman sa lihiya is a chewy banana-leaf-wrapped sticky rice cake best served with coconut caramel or grated coconut and sugar.
ingredients: 1/2 can coconut milk or cream, for latik
3 tablespoons white sugar, for topping, or to taste
1/2 can coconut milk, for latik sauce
steps: Rinse the glutinous rice several times until the water is almost clear, then soak it in 2 cups water overnight.
Drain the soaked rice in a strainer until it no longer drips, transfer to a glass or plastic bowl, mix in the lye water thoroughly, and let stand for 1 hour.
Prepare banana leaves by cutting them into pieces at least 12 inches long, removing the stiff center rib, washing and drying them, then briefly passing each leaf over heat until pliable.

Place about 2 spoonfuls of rice in the center of a banana leaf, fold and close the packet while leaving a little room for expansion, then make a second packet and tie the pair together with cotton string.
Arrange the paired suman in a large pot, cover with water, bring to a boil over high heat, then lower to medium-low, cover, and simmer for about 45 minutes until the rice is cooked and sticky.

For latik, simmer 1/2 can coconut milk or cream uncovered over medium heat, stirring occasionally until reduced; lower the heat and stir constantly until coconut curds form and turn deep caramel brown, then separate from the oil.
For latik sauce, combine 1/2 can coconut milk, brown sugar, and a pinch of salt in a saucepan, bring to a boil over medium heat, then cook with frequent stirring until thick and caramel-like.
Serve the suman warm or cold with latik sauce, latik curds, grated coconut, and white sugar.

intro: Balbacua is a rich, slow-simmered oxtail stew made hearty with beans, saba bananas, peanut butter, and black bean flavor.
ingredients: 1 can baked beans or pork and beans, 400 g
Freshly ground black pepper, to taste
steps: Heat a little oil in a large heavy pot over medium-high heat and brown the oxtail on all sides, then transfer it to a plate.
In the same pot, saute the garlic and onions over medium heat until the onions are soft.
Return the oxtail to the pot, add the water and beef stock, and bring to a boil.
Lower the heat, cover, and simmer gently for about 2 hours and 30 minutes, or until the oxtail is becoming very tender.

Add the saba bananas, leeks, baked beans, peanut butter, tomato paste, black bean paste, and fermented black beans; bring back to a boil, then simmer for 30 minutes more until the sauce is thick and the meat is tender.
Season with fish sauce and freshly ground black pepper, garnish with sliced tomatoes, and serve with rice.

intro: A simple sauté of bitter melon, tomatoes, and soft eggs that makes a quick Filipino vegetable dish for rice.
ingredients: 2 medium ampalaya (bitter melon), halved, seeded, and thinly sliced
Salt and black pepper, to taste
steps: Slice the ampalaya thinly and remove all seeds and white pith. Rinse and drain well.
Heat oil in a pan over medium heat. Cook the onion and garlic until softened, then add the tomatoes and cook until they release their juices.
Add the ampalaya and water. Cover and cook for 3 to 5 minutes, until just tender.
Pour in the beaten eggs and let them set briefly before gently folding them through the vegetables. Season with salt and pepper and serve immediately.

intro: Nilagang pata is a comforting clear soup of tender pork hock, saba, potato, and pechay seasoned simply with patis and peppercorns.
ingredients: 2 lbs pork hock or pata, sliced
2 cups beef stock or beef broth, optional
1 large bunch baby bok choy or pechay
steps: Combine the water and beef stock or broth, if using, in a large pot and bring to a boil.
Add the onion, whole peppercorns, and sliced pork hock, then simmer for about 60 minutes until the pork is tender, adding water as needed to keep it covered.
Add the cubed potato and sliced saba bananas and cook for 10 minutes, or until the potato is tender.
Stir in the fish sauce and baby bok choy or pechay, then turn off the heat, cover the pot, and let the greens wilt in the hot broth for 10 minutes.
Transfer to a serving bowl and serve hot.

intro: Sinigang sa miso brings salmon, vegetables, and mustard greens into a sour broth enriched with savory miso.
steps: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat, then saute the garlic and onion until fragrant; add the ginger and cook briefly until aromatic.
Add the tomatoes and cook until softened, then stir in the miso paste and cook for 2 minutes.
Pour in 6 to 8 cups water, mix well, and bring the broth to a boil.
Add the radish and cook until tender, then stir in the tamarind soup mix and season with salt to taste.
Add the salmon, eggplant, okra, and long chilies, gently moving them through the broth, and cook for about 5 minutes until the fish and vegetables are done.
Add the mustard leaves, cook for 1 minute just until wilted, then remove from heat and serve.

intro: Juicy grilled rib eye with yellow rice makes a simple but festive Filipino-style steak plate with warm spices and chicken broth.
steps: For the arroz amarillo, heat the olive oil in a pot over medium heat, add the long grain rice, and saute for 30 seconds.
Stir in the turmeric, smoked paprika, and 1/4 teaspoon salt until the rice is evenly coated, then pour in the chicken broth.
Bring to a boil, cover, and cook over medium heat for 9 to 11 minutes; lower the heat and continue cooking for 20 to 25 minutes, until the rice has absorbed the liquid.
Mix the steak rub ingredients: 1 1/2 teaspoons salt, cracked peppercorn, garlic powder, and cayenne if using.
Rub the seasoning over both steaks and let them stand for 8 to 12 minutes while the grill heats.
Grill the steaks for 5 to 6 minutes per side for medium-rare, or longer for a more cooked center.
Rest the steaks for 10 minutes before serving with the arroz amarillo.

intro: Beef pater wraps moist turmeric-seasoned shredded brisket and rice in softened banana leaves with palapa on the side.
ingredients: 4 tbsp soy sauce, preferably Silver Swan
3 cups water, plus extra as needed
10 banana leaf squares, 8 x 8 inches, briefly passed over flame to soften
10 cups cooked rice or turmeric rice
steps: Heat the cooking oil in a heavy pot over medium heat, saute the onion until translucent, then add the garlic and cook until fragrant.
Add the beef brisket and sear until the pieces are browned on the outside.
Pour in 3 cups water, scrape the bottom of the pot to loosen browned bits, and bring to a boil.
Lower the heat, cover, and simmer for about 2 hours, adding 1/2 cup hot water at a time if the pot gets too dry, until the beef is tender.
Transfer the beef to a bowl and reserve 1/2 cup of the broth; shred the beef with forks.
Return the shredded beef and reserved broth to the pot, then add soy sauce, oyster sauce, black pepper, turmeric, and sea salt.
Cook uncovered for about 10 minutes, stirring, until most liquid has evaporated but the beef remains moist.
Lay a softened banana leaf square on a flat surface, add 1 cup cooked rice, top with beef, and leave about a 2 cm border.
Fold the leaf lengthwise around the filling, tuck in the ends to make a tight packet, and repeat with the remaining rice and beef.
Serve warm with palapa, either wrapped or opened on the banana leaf.

intro: A cool, creamy dessert salad combining tender buko strips, juicy lychee, and chewy nata de coco.
ingredients: 2 cups lychee, fresh or canned and drained if needed
1 cup coconut jelly (nata de coco), drained
steps: Place the young coconut strips, lychee, and nata de coco in a large mixing bowl.
Add the whipped or thickened cream and condensed milk.
Fold everything together until the fruit and jelly are evenly coated in the cream mixture.
Cover and chill for at least 1 hour before serving so the salad is cold and the flavors settle.
Serve straight from the refrigerator.

intro: Small pompano are scored, seasoned simply, and deep-fried until the skin turns crisp and golden.
ingredients: Freshly ground black pepper, to taste
steps: Score both sides of each pompano, then rub sea salt and freshly ground black pepper over the surface, inside the cavity, and into the cuts.
Pat the fish very dry with paper towels to reduce splattering and help the skin crisp.
Heat enough oil for deep-frying in a wok or deep pan to 180°C over medium-high heat.
Carefully lower the fish into the hot oil without crowding and fry for about 7 minutes per side, or until golden brown, crisp, and cooked through.
Lift out the fish, drain well on a rack or paper towels, and serve hot.

intro: This quick sinabawang corned beef turns canned corned beef, potato, and aromatics into a comforting saucy ulam.
steps: Heat the cooking oil in a pan over medium heat, then saute the garlic and onion until the onion is soft.
Add the corned beef and cook for 3 minutes, stirring to loosen and heat it evenly.
Add the potato and cook for 5 minutes, stirring occasionally so it absorbs flavor without sticking.
Pour in the water and bring to a boil, then lower the heat and simmer until the potato is tender and the liquid reduces by about half; add more water if you want it soupier.
Stir in half of the parsley, then season with salt and pepper.
Transfer to a serving bowl and top with the remaining parsley.

intro: This generous goto pairs beef innards rice porridge with crisp tofu and pork cheeks in a tangy soy-vinegar sauce.
ingredients: 4 quarts water, plus 2 quarts for parboiling innards
Salt and ground black pepper, to taste
1/4 cup chopped green onion, for sauce
1/2 cup lemon-lime soda, shaken to release fizz
steps: For the innards, boil 2 quarts water in a pot with 3 stalks lemongrass and 4 dried bay leaves; add the beef heart, ox tripe, and beef large intestine and boil for 30 minutes, then discard the liquid and set the innards aside.
Heat 4 tbsp cooking oil in a large pot over medium heat, saute the minced garlic until lightly browned, then add the onion and ginger and cook until the onion softens.
Add the jasmine rice and glutinous rice and stir for 1 to 2 minutes to coat the grains.
Pour in 4 quarts water, bring to a boil, then stir in the beef cubes and fish sauce.

Add the parboiled innards, cover, and cook over low to medium heat, stirring every few minutes, for up to 90 minutes or until the innards are very tender and the rice has broken down into a porridge; add water as needed to keep it loose.
Season the goto with onion powder, turmeric powder, salt, toasted garlic, and ground black pepper, then keep it warm.
Make the sauce by mixing the sliced red onion, Thai chilies, 1/4 cup green onion, chopped garlic, soy sauce, white vinegar, defizzed lemon-lime soda, salt, and pepper in a bowl; set aside.
For the tokwa't baboy, boil 1 quart water with the pig cheeks, 2 stalks lemongrass, 3 dried bay leaves, and 1 tbsp salt over medium heat for 45 minutes, then remove the pork and let it cool.
Heat 1/2 cup oil in a pan and fry the pork cheeks for about 2 minutes per side, or until browned; remove and set aside.
Add the remaining oil to the pan and deep-fry the extra-firm tofu, turning as needed, until golden brown on all sides.
Slice the pork and tofu into serving pieces, arrange them with red onion, and spoon over a generous amount of sauce.
Serve the hot goto in bowls topped with green onion, toasted garlic, and chili garlic oil, with the tokwa't baboy on the side.

intro: Pan de regla is a soft Filipino bread filled with a bright red milk-bread pudding center.
ingredients: 10 to 12 medium-thick slices bread, roughly torn
1 tbsp red food coloring, or enough for a bright red color
steps: Combine the lukewarm water, yeast, and 1/2 tbsp of the sugar in a bowl, then let it stand in a warm spot until foamy.
In a large mixing bowl, combine the high-grade flour, lukewarm milk, melted butter, remaining sugar, salt, and the foamy yeast mixture.
Knead with a dough hook on the lowest speed for 5 minutes until a dough forms, then knead on medium speed for about 20 minutes until smooth and elastic.
Cover the bowl with a clean damp towel and let the dough rise in a warm place until doubled.
While the dough rises, pulse the torn bread and full-cream milk in a food processor until loose and pasty.

Transfer the bread mixture to a large nonstick pan, add the beaten eggs, 3/4 cup sugar, red food coloring, 3 tbsp butter, and vanilla, then cook over medium heat while stirring constantly until thick, dense, and pudding-like; cool completely.
Deflate the risen dough, flatten it, and divide it into 2 equal portions.
Roll one portion into a rectangle, place filling along the middle of the upper half and the middle of the lower half, then slice the dough crosswise between the two filled sections.
Pull the edges of each filled half together to seal, place seam-side down, and cut into 9 pieces; arrange on a baking-paper-lined tray and poke the tops with a fork.
Repeat with the second dough portion to make 36 pieces total, then loosely cover and let rise for about 1 hour, or until puffy.
Brush the tops with beaten egg wash.
Bake in a preheated 180°C oven for 15 to 18 minutes, or until the tops are golden brown.

intro: Chicken paksiw gives leftover chicken a savory-sour second life with vinegar, lechon sauce, aromatics, and bay leaves.
ingredients: 1 lb leftover chicken, cut into pieces
steps: Heat the cooking oil in a pan over medium heat, then saute the onion and garlic until the onion softens.
Add the chicken pieces and saute for 1 minute to coat them with the aromatics.
Pour in the lechon sauce and vinegar, then let the mixture come to a boil before stirring.
Add the water and bring it back to a boil.
Stir in the chicken cube, bay leaves, and whole peppercorns, then cover the pan, lower the heat to the lowest setting, and cook for 35 minutes.
Uncover and continue simmering until the sauce reduces by about half.
Add the sugar, season with salt, and stir until the sauce is balanced and glossy.
Transfer to a serving bowl and serve with warm rice.

intro: Filipino pork chop steak simmers pan-fried marinated chops in a calamansi-soy sauce with plenty of onions.
steps: Combine the pork chops, soy sauce, and lime or calamansi juice in a bowl or resealable bag and marinate for at least 1 hour.
Heat the cooking oil in a pan over medium heat.
Remove the pork chops from the marinade, reserving the marinade, and pan-fry the chops for 3 minutes per side; transfer them to a plate.
Using the remaining oil in the pan, saute the garlic until it starts to brown.
Add half of the sliced onions and cook until softened.
Pour in the reserved marinade and water, then return the pork chops to the pan.
Simmer for about 45 minutes, adding more water as needed, until the pork is tender.
Stir in the sugar, then season with salt and ground black pepper.
Add the remaining onions and cook for 3 minutes more, just until slightly softened.
Turn off the heat and serve the pork chops with the sauce and onions.

intro: Sinantomas is a comforting Quezon-style pork stew with pineapple, tomato, sweet potatoes, peas, peppers, and cheese in a savory-sweet sauce.
ingredients: 1 kg pork spareribs, cut into sections
3 tablespoons fish sauce, plus more to season
Freshly ground black pepper, to taste
steps: In a large bowl or container, combine the pork spareribs, pineapple juice, soy sauce, and 3 tablespoons fish sauce. Cover and marinate for at least 2 hours.
Heat oil in a pot over medium heat. Saute the garlic and onions until fragrant, then add the tomatoes and cook for about 2 minutes, until softened.
Add the pork together with all the marinade, then pour in the chicken stock. Bring to a boil, lower the heat, cover partially, and simmer for about 45 minutes, or until the ribs are becoming tender.
Add the sweet potatoes, green peas, green capsicum, tomato sauce, and tomato catsup. Continue simmering for 10 to 15 minutes, until the sweet potatoes are tender but not falling apart.
Stir in the grated cheddar cheese until melted into the sauce. Taste and adjust with more fish sauce if needed, then finish with freshly ground black pepper and serve hot.

intro: These crispy ham and cheese bread rolls are simple merienda bites with a molten center and golden breadcrumb coating.
steps: Flatten each slice of bread with a rolling pin or clean bottle. Lay 1 piece of ham and 1 slice of cheddar on each bread slice, then roll tightly and place seam-side down.
Put the beaten eggs in one shallow dish and the bread crumbs in another. Dip each roll in egg, then coat evenly with bread crumbs, pressing gently so the coating sticks.
Heat enough oil in a frying pan to cover the surface over medium heat. Fry the rolls seam-side down first so they seal, then turn as needed until all sides are golden brown.
Drain the cooked rolls on a paper towel-lined plate to remove excess oil. Slice each roll diagonally in half and serve hot.

intro: Bulalo steak turns tender beef shanks into a sizzling plate dish with mushroom gravy and fried onions.
ingredients: 1 head garlic, pounded with skin on
1 1/2 cups reduced beef stock from boiling the shanks
Freshly ground black pepper, to taste
steps: Place the beef shanks, pounded garlic, quartered onions, peppercorns, rubbed parsley, and salt in a pot. Add just enough water to barely cover, bring to a boil, then lower the heat and simmer for 1 1/2 to 2 hours, until the beef is tender.
Remove the shanks and set them aside. Continue boiling the broth until reduced, then strain it through muslin or a fine strainer and measure 1 1/2 cups for the gravy.
In a pan, melt 2 tablespoons butter over medium heat. Cook the sliced mushrooms until tender and lightly browned, then remove and set aside.
In the same pan, melt 3 tablespoons butter and saute the minced garlic for about 1 minute. Stir in the mushroom powder for another minute, then add the flour and mix into a roux.
Pour in the Worcestershire sauce and reduced beef stock, then add the onion powder. Cook, stirring, until the gravy thickens; season with salt and freshly ground black pepper.
Heat a sizzling plate on the stovetop over high heat. Lightly brush the tender beef shanks with oil, place them on the hot plate, and sear for 3 to 4 minutes per side.
Top the shanks with the cooked mushrooms, pour the hot gravy over them, add fried onions, and serve while sizzling.

intro: A hearty pork adobo made richer with fried tokwa and tausi, served with garlicky adobo fried rice for a complete Filipino meal.
steps: Make the toasted garlic first: put the cooking oil and crushed garlic in a pan, warm over low heat, and cook gently until the garlic is golden. Lift out the toasted garlic and reserve both the garlic and the flavored oil.
Heat about half of the garlic oil in a pan over medium heat. Add the pork and saute until the pieces are lightly browned on the outside.

Add the soy sauce, vinegar, bay leaves, peppercorns, salted black beans, and water. Bring to a boil, then cover, lower the heat to a steady simmer, and cook for about 40 minutes, or until the pork is tender.

Stir in the fried tofu and brown sugar. Cook for about 3 minutes more, just until the tofu absorbs some sauce and the seasoning balances. Transfer the adobo to a serving dish, reserving 3 tablespoons sauce for the rice.
For the fried rice, gently toss the leftover rice with the salt to break up clumps. Heat the remaining garlic oil and toasted garlic in a wide pan over medium-high heat.

Add the rice and drizzle in the 3 tablespoons adobo sauce. Stir-fry for 3 to 5 minutes, until the grains are hot, evenly coated, and lightly glossy. Serve the garlic fried rice with the pork adobo and tokwa.

intro: This quick ginisang repolyo turns cabbage, chicken, and bell peppers into a light but flavorful everyday ulam.
ingredients: 4 ounces boneless chicken breast, thinly sliced
1 small red bell pepper, sliced into strips
1 small green bell pepper, sliced into strips
Salt and ground black pepper, to taste
steps: Heat the cooking oil in a pot or deep pan over medium heat. Saute the onion and garlic until the onion softens.
Add the sliced chicken and cook, stirring, until the chicken changes color and lightly browns in spots.
Pour in 3/4 cup water and bring to a boil. Add the Knorr Chicken Cube, cover, and cook until the liquid is mostly absorbed and the chicken is cooked through.
Add the oyster sauce and cabbage, then stir-fry for about 1 minute to coat the cabbage.
Pour in the remaining 1/2 cup water. Stir, cover if needed, and cook for about 5 minutes, until the cabbage is tender but still has some bite.
Add the red and green bell peppers. Season with salt and ground black pepper, then cook for 2 minutes more, just until the peppers are crisp-tender. Transfer to a plate and serve.

intro: Pata Linaga Salamukan Style is a slow-simmered pork hock and beef tendon soup brightened with annatto, lemongrass, citrus, and gentle chili heat.
ingredients: 2 kg pork hock, cut into sections
200 ml Mountain Dew or lime soda
2 stalks lemongrass, pounded and tied in a knot
2 to 3 red chillies, whole or sliced
Freshly ground black pepper, to taste
steps: Heat about 3 tablespoons oil in a small saucepan over low heat. Add the annatto seeds and stir until the oil turns deep red, then strain and discard the seeds.
Warm the annatto oil in a large pot over medium heat. Saute the garlic and onion until fragrant and the onion looks translucent.

Add the sliced beef tendon and saute for a few minutes so it picks up the aromatics. Pour in enough water to cover the tendon, then add the celery, lemongrass, and chillies. Season lightly with salt and black pepper.
Cover, bring to a boil, then lower the heat and simmer for about 1 1/2 hours.
Add the pork hock, pour in the 200 ml Mountain Dew, and add more water as needed so the meat and tendon stay submerged. Bring back to a boil, then reduce to low heat.
Cover and simmer for another 2 to 3 hours, adding water when needed, until the pork hock is tender and the tendon is very soft and gelatinous.
Remove the lemongrass and whole chillies if used. Stir in the lemon juice and fish sauce, then adjust with more salt, pepper, or fish sauce to taste.
Serve in bowls with pork hock, beef tendon, and plenty of hot broth; add extra sliced chillies if desired.

intro: Seafood kare-kare keeps the peanut-rich comfort of the classic dish while using shrimp, crab, mussels, and squid for a festive pot.
ingredients: 1/2 lb mussels, boiled in 3/4 cup water, liquid reserved
1 1/2 tablespoons annatto powder, diluted in 3 tablespoons water
steps: Bring 5 cups water to a boil in a pot. Blanch the string beans and banana heart for 3 to 4 minutes, then transfer them to ice water for 3 minutes. Drain and set aside.
Heat 3 tablespoons oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Pan-fry the shrimp for 2 minutes per side, then remove and set aside.

In the same pan, fry the squid for 2 minutes per side only, then remove so it stays tender. Fry the steamed crabs for about 2 1/2 minutes per side, adding a little oil if the pan gets dry, then set aside.

Add the mussels to the same pan and stir-fry for about 4 minutes total. Pour in the reserved mussel liquid and scrape the browned seafood bits from the pan into the liquid. Remove the mussels and save the liquid separately.
In a clay pot or regular pot, heat the remaining 3 tablespoons oil over medium heat. Saute the garlic and onion until the onion softens.
Pour in the coconut cream and bring it to a gentle boil. Add the reserved seafood liquid, then stir in the peanut butter until fully dissolved.
Season with fish sauce, then stir in the diluted annatto. Cook over medium heat for 2 to 5 minutes, stirring, until the sauce is smooth and colored.
Arrange the blanched vegetables and cooked seafood in the sauce, warming them briefly if needed. Top or serve with shrimp paste on the side.

intro: Pininat is a rich baked kakanin with coconut milk, macapuno, and milks folded into a chewy rice-flour batter.
steps: Preheat the oven to 180 C and line a large baking tray with banana leaves.
In a large bowl, combine the coconut milk, condensed milk, evaporated milk, melted butter, eggs, macapuno, vanilla extract, and salt. Mix on medium speed until smooth and even.
Add the glutinous rice flour gradually, mixing after each addition until the batter is fully combined and free of dry pockets.
Pour the batter into the prepared tray and spread it level.
Bake for 45 to 50 minutes, until the top is golden brown and the center is set. Cool before slicing and serving.

intro: Monok is a savory shredded mixed-meat dish marinated in vinegar, soy sauce, garlic, onion, and chilies, then pan-fried until browned and crisp-edged.
ingredients: 1 kg flaked cooked meat, a mix of chicken, pork, and beef
steps: Place the flaked cooked chicken, pork, and beef in a large bowl.
In a separate bowl, mix the cane vinegar, soy sauce, crumbled chicken bouillon cube, red onion, 6 cloves minced garlic, and chopped red chillies until combined.
Pour the marinade over the flaked meat and mix well so the meat is evenly coated. Cover and refrigerate for at least 1 hour; marinate overnight for a stronger flavor if time allows.
Heat the oil in a large pan over medium heat. Add the white onion and the remaining 6 cloves minced garlic, then saute until fragrant and the onion turns translucent.
Add the marinated meat along with its liquid. Stir-fry until the liquid reduces, the meat is heated through, and the strands begin to brown.

Sprinkle in the brown sugar and keep sauteing for a few more minutes, until the edges become lightly crisp and caramelized. Taste and adjust with extra soy sauce or vinegar only if needed, then serve hot with steamed rice.

intro: Spicy ginataang hipon is a fast shrimp dish with creamy gata, ginger, green pepper, and labuyo heat.
ingredients: 1 1/2 lb medium shrimp, heads and shells on
steps: In a bowl, dissolve the Knorr Ginataang Gulay mix in the lukewarm water and set the gata mixture aside.
Heat the cooking oil in a pot over medium heat. Saute the garlic, onion, and ginger until fragrant and the onion begins to soften.
Add the long green peppers, scallions, and chopped chilies. Stir and cook for about 1 minute.
Pour in the gata mixture and bring it to a boil. Add the shrimp and cook, stirring occasionally, for about 5 minutes, until the shells turn orange and the shrimp are just cooked through.
Season with ground black pepper and fish sauce if using. Stir and cook for 1 to 2 minutes more, then transfer to a bowl and serve with rice.

intro: Kinalabasang Sugpo is a creamy coconut prawn dish where squash softens into the sauce and chilies add gentle heat.
ingredients: 1/4 medium butternut squash, cut into cubes
1 tightly packed cup malunggay leaves or baby spinach, optional
steps: Heat oil in a wok over medium heat, then saute the garlic and red onion until fragrant and softened.
Add the cubed squash and pan-fry gently for 5 minutes, turning carefully so the pieces begin to soften without breaking apart.
Pour in the chicken stock and add the green long chilies. Cover, bring to a boil, and simmer over high heat for 5 minutes.
Add the prawns, malunggay leaves or baby spinach if using, and coconut milk. Stir gently and simmer over medium heat for 10 minutes, until the prawns are cooked and the squash is tender.
Season with fish sauce and black pepper to taste, then serve hot.

intro: Piaparan pairs tender simmered chicken with a turmeric-coconut coating and a light coconut broth served alongside it.
steps: Make the palapa by pounding the finely chopped spring onions, ginger paste, and bird's eye chilies in a mortar until paste-like; set aside.
Heat oil in a pot over medium heat, then saute the garlic and red onions until softened and aromatic. Stir in 1 tablespoon of the palapa and cook briefly until fragrant.
Add the chicken legs and salt, turning the pieces until lightly browned on all sides. Pour in the water, bring to a boil, then lower to a simmer and cook for 25 minutes.

Lift the chicken from the pot and set it aside. Add the chayote to the broth and cook for 5 minutes, then stir in the coconut milk and simmer for another 5 minutes. Add the chopped spring onions and turn off the heat.

While the soup finishes, heat oil in a wok and saute the remaining palapa. Add the turmeric, shredded coconut, red capsicum, and green capsicum, stir-frying until the coconut is evenly yellow and fragrant.
Add the cooked chicken to the coconut mixture and turn to coat well. Cover the wok and cook over low heat for 10 minutes, until the coating clings to the chicken and the meat is heated through.
Serve the coconut-coated chicken on a platter with the coconut-chayote soup on the side.

intro: This beef and ampalaya stir-fry balances tender marinated sirloin with crisp bitter gourd and savory oyster sauce.
ingredients: 1/2 lb beef sirloin, sliced into thin strips
1 medium bitter gourd, cored and sliced
2 tablespoons sherry or Shaoxing cooking wine
steps: In a bowl, combine the beef, soy sauce, sherry or Shaoxing wine, sesame oil, and ground black pepper. Mix well, then add the cornstarch and toss until the beef is evenly coated.
Heat 3 tablespoons cooking oil in a wok or pan over high heat. Stir-fry the beef for 4 to 6 minutes, until browned, then transfer it to a clean plate.
Add the remaining 1 tablespoon oil to the same pan. Stir-fry the sliced ampalaya for about 2 minutes, keeping it crisp-tender.
Pour in the oyster sauce and stir-fry for 30 seconds to coat the ampalaya.
Return the beef to the pan and cook for 1 minute more, tossing everything together until hot and glossy. Transfer to a serving plate and serve with warm rice.

intro: Lengua de Gato are thin Filipino butter cookies baked until crisp with pale centers and lightly golden edges.
steps: Preheat the oven to 180 C and line a baking pan with baking paper.
Cream the softened butter in a mixing bowl with an electric mixer for 1 minute, then add the caster sugar gradually and continue mixing for about 2 minutes.
Add the egg whites and beat for 2 minutes more. Add the sifted flour gradually and mix for another 2 minutes, then blend in the vanilla and salt for 1 minute.
Transfer the batter to a piping bag fitted with a large flat oval tip. Pipe strips about 3 inches long onto the lined pan, leaving space between them.
Bake for about 10 minutes, until the edges turn light golden brown while the centers remain pale. Let the cookies cool before serving.

intro: Inipit is a soft Filipino sponge sandwich filled with a sweet potato custard and finished in neat rectangular slices.
steps: Preheat the oven to 160 C and grease two rectangular 12 x 9-inch pans.
Beat the 6 egg whites with the cream of tartar on high speed until soft peaks form. Gradually beat in 1/2 cup of the sugar and continue until stiff peaks form; set aside.
In another bowl, mix the 6 egg yolks, fresh milk, remaining 1 cup sugar, vanilla extract, and salt until creamy.
Sift together the flour and baking powder, then mix them into the yolk mixture. Fold in the beaten egg whites gently until combined.
Divide the batter evenly between the prepared pans. Bake for 35 minutes, or until a toothpick inserted in the center comes out clean.

While the cakes bake, make the filling: combine the mashed potato, 2/3 cup sugar, condensed milk, milk, butter, and lemon rind in a saucepan. Cook over medium heat for about 15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until thickened.
Lower the heat, add the 3 egg yolks, and cook for 5 minutes more while stirring constantly. Let the custard and the sponge cakes cool.
Remove one cake layer from its pan and place it on a flat tray. Spread the potato custard over it, top with the second cake layer, and press lightly so the layers settle together.
Slice into small rectangles, dust with powdered sugar, and serve.

intro: Nilagang Baboy is a clear, comforting pork soup built from long-simmered bones, tender ribs, sweet potatoes, saba, and bok choy.
ingredients: 3 saba bananas, cut into 3 sections each
Freshly ground black pepper, to taste
steps: In a deep pot, combine the pork bones, red onions, celery, carrot, peppercorns, salt, and water. Heat until nearly boiling, skim off the scum that rises, then simmer over low heat for 3 hours.
Add the pork ribs to the pot and simmer for 30 minutes more.
Remove the pork ribs and set them aside. Strain the broth through a fine strainer into a clean pot.
Bring the strained stock to a boil, then cook over medium-high heat for 15 minutes to reduce and concentrate it.
Return the pork ribs to the pot and add the white onions. Lower the heat and simmer for 30 minutes.
Add the saba bananas and sweet potatoes, then simmer for 10 to 15 minutes, until the sweet potatoes are tender.
Turn off the heat, add the bok choy, season with fish sauce, and cover the pot for 5 minutes so the greens wilt in the hot broth.
Finish with freshly ground black pepper and serve in bowls garnished with chopped spring onions.

intro: This Kapampangan-style mung bean stew is creamy, savory, and rich with bagoong, tender lechon, greens, and crunchy chicharon.
ingredients: 1 teaspoon salt, plus more to taste
500 g lechon or lechon kawali, chopped
Freshly ground black pepper, to taste
steps: Rinse the mung beans, then place them in a pot with 6 cups water and 1 teaspoon salt. Simmer over medium-low heat for 30 to 40 minutes, until the beans are very soft.
Lightly mash the cooked mung beans until partly creamy but still textured, then set them aside.
Heat the oil in a large pan over medium heat. Saute the onion until softened, then add the garlic and cook just until fragrant.
Add the tomatoes and cook, stirring often, until they soften and break down into the aromatics.
Stir in the bagoong alamang and cook for about 3 minutes to round out its flavor.
Add the chopped lechon or lechon kawali and toss until coated; let it cook briefly so some fat renders into the pan.
Pour in the mashed mung beans and stir well. Add a little water or stock if the mixture is too thick, then simmer for 20 minutes, stirring occasionally.
Fold in the baby spinach and cook just until wilted. Season with salt and freshly ground black pepper, then stir in or sprinkle over the crushed chicharon before serving with steamed rice.

intro: Adobong Isaw ng Baboy is a bold, garlicky pork intestine adobo simmered tender first, then reduced in a savory vinegar-soy sauce.
steps: Put the cleaned pork intestines, salt, crushed ginger, and water in a wok. Cover, bring to a boil, then lower the heat and simmer for 90 minutes, or until the intestines are tender.
Remove the intestines, rinse them well under running water, and cut into serving pieces.

In a clean wok, combine the crushed garlic and cooking oil. Cook over low heat until the garlic turns golden, then strain out the garlic and reserve both the toasted garlic and the garlic oil separately.
Return 3 tablespoons of the garlic oil to the wok and add 2 teaspoons of the toasted garlic. Heat the pan, then add the sliced intestines and saute until browned.
Pour in the soy sauce, then add the cracked peppercorns and bay leaves. Add the vinegar and let it come to a boil before stirring.
Add the beef broth and simmer until the liquid reduces to about one quarter of its original volume.
Stir in the brown sugar and chopped Thai chilies. Add the oyster sauce, green onions, and remaining toasted garlic, then cook for 30 seconds more.
Transfer to a serving plate and serve hot.

intro: Napoleones are flaky layered puff pastry squares filled with vanilla custard and finished with a smooth milk-sugar glaze.
steps: Stack the 3 puff pastry sheets into one layered slab, then cut into 9 equal squares by slicing 3 rows by 3 rows. Chill the cut pastry while preparing the custard.
In a pot, combine the milk, cream, and 1/4 cup sugar. Warm over medium heat until it reaches a gentle boil, then lower the heat.
In a bowl, sift together the remaining 1/4 cup sugar and cornstarch. Whisk in the egg yolks until smooth.
Slowly whisk about 1 cup of the hot milk mixture into the yolk mixture to temper it, then pour everything back into the pot.
Cook the custard over low heat, whisking constantly, for 4 to 5 minutes, until thick enough to hold soft lines from the whisk.
Turn off the heat, then whisk in the butter and vanilla until fully incorporated. Transfer to a bowl, press plastic wrap onto the surface, and let cool.
Heat the oven to 180 C. Arrange the chilled pastry pieces on a baking pan and bake for about 45 minutes, until puffed and golden brown. Cool completely.
For the glaze, place the icing sugar in a bowl and mix in the fresh milk 1 tablespoon at a time until thick, silky, and pourable.
Using a bread knife, split each cooled pastry through the middle. Fill with custard, close the pastry, and drizzle the glaze over the top before serving.

intro: Bangus ala Pobre is fried milkfish belly coated in a glossy soy-calamansi sauce and topped with onions and toasted garlic.
ingredients: 500 g boneless bangus belly, cut into serving pieces
1 big yellow onion, cut into rings
1 teaspoon cornstarch, from the leftover dredge
steps: Heat enough oil for shallow-frying in a skillet over medium-high heat.
Season the bangus belly pieces lightly with salt and pepper, then dredge them in the 1/4 cup cornstarch and shake off the excess.
Fry the fish skin-side down first, turning once, until both sides are golden brown and the fish is cooked through. Remove and set aside.
Lower the heat to medium-low and toast the minced garlic in the same oil until golden. Remove the garlic promptly with a sieve and set aside, keeping the oil in the pan.
In a bowl, mix the soy sauce, oyster sauce if using, lemon or calamansi juice, 1 teaspoon cornstarch, and water until smooth.
Cook the onion rings in the same oil over medium heat until softened, then remove and set aside.
Add the butter to the skillet and let it melt into the remaining oil. Pour in the sauce mixture and cook, stirring, until thickened.
Return the fried bangus to the pan and turn gently to coat with sauce. Transfer to a serving dish, pour the remaining sauce over the fish, and top with the onions and toasted garlic.

intro: Ginataang Langka with Malunggay and Dilis is a quick coconut vegetable dish with savory dried anchovies and leafy malunggay.
steps: Heat the cooking oil in a pan over medium heat.
Add the dried anchovies and cook for 30 seconds, stirring so they flavor the oil without burning.
Add the young jackfruit and saute for 3 minutes.
Pour in the coconut milk and add the Thai chili peppers. Stir, cover, and cook over medium heat until the sauce reduces by half.
Add the malunggay leaves and continue cooking until the coconut milk has mostly evaporated and the leaves are wilted.
Season with fish sauce and ground black pepper, then serve with warm rice.

intro: Pork Ribs Sinigang is a sour tamarind pork soup with tender ribs, radish, okra, eggplant, string beans, chilies, and bok choy.
ingredients: 44 g Knorr Sinigang sa Sampaloc with Gabi
steps: Heat the cooking oil in a large pot over medium heat. Saute the onion and tomatoes until the onion layers begin to separate.
Add the pork ribs and continue sauteing until the meat turns light brown.
Pour in the water, cover the pot, and bring to a boil. Lower the heat and simmer for 30 minutes.
Stir in the sinigang mix and daikon radish. Cover and continue cooking until the pork is tender.
Add the long green chilies, string beans, okra, and eggplant, then cook for 12 minutes.
Add the bok choy and cook for 3 minutes, just until wilted and tender-crisp.
Season with fish sauce and ground black pepper, then serve hot with rice.

intro: Squid sisig is a quick, smoky seafood pulutan tossed with soy, aromatics, chilies, mayonnaise, and lemon.
ingredients: 1 to 2 bird's eye chilies, finely chopped
Freshly ground black pepper, to taste
steps: Heat a grill to high. Grill the cleaned squid briefly, about 2 minutes or less per side, just until firm; avoid cooking it until tough.
Let the grilled squid cool slightly, then chop it into small pieces.
In a large bowl, mix the soy sauce, garlic, ginger, bird's eye chilies, freshly ground black pepper, and 3 tablespoons oil. Add the chopped squid and toss until coated.
Heat a heavy-bottomed pan over high heat until very hot and lightly smoking. Add the squid mixture and stir-fry quickly for 1 to 2 minutes only.
Transfer the squid to a bowl, season with salt, then mix in the minced onions and mayonnaise.
Serve immediately with lemon wedges for squeezing over the sisig.

intro: Simple grilled galunggong becomes a satisfying Filipino meal when paired with smoky mashed eggplant salad brightened with calamansi and bagoong.
steps: Rub the galunggong all over with coarse sea salt, including inside the cavity, and let the fish stand for 15 minutes.

While the fish seasons, prick the eggplant all over with a fork and place it directly over a medium open flame. Turn it about every minute until the skin is charred all around, the flesh is soft, and steam escapes from the eggplant.
Let the eggplant cool until safe to handle, then peel away the burnt skin, remove the stem, and roughly chop or mash the flesh.
In a bowl, combine the eggplant, tomato, red onion, calamansi juice, bagoong alamang, and black pepper. Mix well and set aside.
Heat a grill to medium-high. Thread each fish onto bamboo skewers if desired, then brush lightly with oil so the skin releases more easily.
Grill the galunggong for 4 to 5 minutes per side, turning once, until the flesh is opaque and cooked through. Serve hot with the ensaladang talong, rice, and vinegar dip if desired.

intro: Ginisang okra at dilis is a budget-friendly saute with crisp dried anchovies, tender okra, tomatoes, and garlic.
ingredients: Freshly ground black pepper, to taste
steps: Heat oil in a wok over medium heat. Stir-fry the dried dilis until fragrant and crisp, then remove them from the wok and set aside.
Using the same wok, lower the heat and saute the garlic and onion until the onion is soft.
Add the chopped tomatoes and cook for about 2 minutes, stirring until they begin to soften.
Return the dilis to the wok, then add the okra and 1/2 cup water. Raise the heat to high and bring to a boil while stir-frying for 5 minutes.
Season with fish sauce and freshly ground black pepper. Lower the heat, cover the wok, and cook for 5 minutes more, until the okra is tender.
Turn off the heat and serve hot with rice.

intro: Ensaladang pako is a crisp, tangy Filipino fern salad with tomatoes, onion, and salted egg in a lightly sweet vinegar dressing.
steps: Place the fiddlehead fern tips in cold water for several minutes, swishing gently to loosen any grit, then rinse well and drain. If preferred, briefly blanch them in boiling water, then cool and drain thoroughly.
In a small bowl, stir the white vinegar, sugar, and freshly ground pepper until the sugar dissolves.
In a large bowl, combine the drained fiddlehead fern, sliced tomatoes, and sliced onion.
Pour the vinegar dressing over the vegetables and toss until evenly coated.
Add the cubed salted eggs last and toss gently so the pieces stay mostly intact. Serve right away.

intro: This pulutan-style beef caldereta is a hearty, spicy stew with tender beef neck bones, tomato sauce, peanut butter, liver spread, and fried vegetables.
steps: Heat the cooking oil in a pressure cooker or heavy pot over medium heat. Saute the onion and garlic until the onion softens.
Add the beef neck bones and cook, turning the pieces, until the outside is lightly browned.
Stir in the soy sauce, tomato sauce, and water, then bring the mixture to a boil.
Add the Knorr Beef Cube, cover the pressure cooker, and cook under pressure for 30 minutes, or until the beef is tender. Release pressure safely before opening.
While the beef cooks, pan-fry the potato and carrot in a separate pan over medium heat until lightly browned, then set aside.
Stir the chopped Thai chilies, liver spread, and peanut butter into the beef stew until the sauce looks smooth and rich.
Add the sliced bell peppers, fried potato, and fried carrot. Cover and cook for 5 to 7 minutes more, until the vegetables are tender but not mushy.
Season with salt and ground black pepper to taste, then serve hot as pulutan or with rice.

intro: Hamonadong baboy is a sweet-savory pork hock dish slowly braised in pineapple juice, soy sauce, brown sugar, and pineapple slices.
steps: Combine the pineapple juice and soy sauce, then place the pork ham hock in a large resealable bag and pour in the marinade. Seal well and refrigerate overnight.
Heat the cooking oil in a large pan or pot over medium heat. Saute the onion and garlic until the onion softens and the garlic begins to turn golden.
Add the marinated pork, reserving the marinade. Sear for 1 minute on one side, then turn and sear the other side for another minute.
Pour in the reserved marinade and add enough water, 3 to 5 cups, to braise the pork. Bring to a boil.
Add the Knorr Pork Cube and stir to dissolve. Cover and cook over low to medium heat for 1 hour.
Turn the ham hock over, cover again, and continue cooking for another hour, until the meat is tender.
Add the brown sugar and pineapple slices, then cover and simmer for 15 minutes more.
Season with ground black pepper and continue cooking uncovered as needed until the sauce reduces by about half and coats the pork. Serve warm.

intro: Filipino sweet macaroni salad is a creamy chilled dessert salad loaded with fruit cocktail, pineapple, kaong, nata de coco, raisins, and cheese.
ingredients: 250 g elbow macaroni, cooked 1 minute less than package directions
400 g can fruit cocktail in heavy syrup, drained
340 g bottle red nata de coco, drained
steps: Cook the elbow macaroni until slightly underdone by about 1 minute, then drain well and cool completely.
In a large mixing bowl, stir together the condensed milk and mayonnaise until smooth.
Add the cooled macaroni, drained fruit cocktail, drained pineapple chunks, raisins, drained green kaong, drained red nata de coco, and cubed cheddar cheese.
Fold gently until every ingredient is evenly coated with the creamy dressing.
Cover and chill before serving so the salad is cold and the flavors settle.

intro: Beef tinola gives the familiar ginger broth a heartier feel with pressure-cooked beef, green papaya, chilies, and leafy greens.
ingredients: 1 small green papaya, cut into wedges
steps: Heat the cooking oil in a pressure cooker over medium heat. Add the garlic and onion and saute for about 30 seconds.
Add the ginger strips and continue cooking until the onion softens and the aromatics smell fragrant.
Add the beef chuck and cook, stirring occasionally, until the pieces are browned on the outside.
Pour in the beef broth and water, then bring the liquid to a boil.
Cover the pressure cooker and cook under pressure for 40 minutes, or until the beef is tender. Release pressure safely before opening.
Add the green papaya wedges and long green chili peppers, if using, then simmer uncovered for 8 to 10 minutes, until the papaya is tender.
Season with fish sauce and ground black pepper, stirring to combine.
Turn off the heat, add the spinach or malunggay leaves, and let the residual heat wilt the greens for about 3 minutes. Serve hot.

intro: Pospas de Gallina is a hearty chicken rice porridge with ginger, kasubha, and toppings, ideal for cool or rainy days.
ingredients: 1 1/2 kg chicken legs, thighs, and/or wings
Freshly ground black pepper, to taste
steps: Heat oil in a large pot over medium-high heat and brown the chicken pieces on all sides until the skin and meat are colored.
Push the chicken to one side of the pot. Add the garlic, onion, and ginger, then sauté over medium heat for a few minutes until fragrant.
Add the chicken stock, water, kasubha, and rice. Bring to a boil, then lower to a simmer and cook for about 40 minutes, stirring every 5 minutes so the rice does not stick to the bottom.
Once the rice is tender and the broth is thick, season with fish sauce and freshly ground black pepper, then turn off the heat.
Ladle the porridge and chicken into bowls. Top with hard-boiled egg, spring onions, and fried garlic, and serve with lemon on the side.

intro: A savory, spicy dish that combines the salty depth of bagoong, tender eggplant, and crisp bagnet.
ingredients: 1 lb bagnet or crispy pork belly, cut into serving pieces
steps: Heat the cooking oil in a pot over medium heat. Sauté the garlic, onion, and tomato until the onion and tomato soften.
Stir in the bagoong alamang and cook briefly to release its flavor. Pour in the water and vinegar, then bring to a boil.
Add the sliced eggplant, Serrano peppers, and half of the bagnet. Cover and cook over low to medium heat until the eggplant is tender and the sauce has reduced by about half, about 20 to 25 minutes.
Season with ground black pepper and sugar, stir, and taste for the salt-sweet balance.
Transfer to a serving plate and top with the remaining bagnet to keep it crisp. Serve hot with rice.

intro: This recipe turns leftover lechon into crisp hand-held snacks with a sweet-savory glaze, cheese, and fresh coriander.
ingredients: 1 1/2 cups leftover Filipino lechon, recooked and shredded
12 small corn tortillas, or flour tortillas
12 processed cheese squares, cut in half
steps: In a skillet over medium heat, sauté the minced garlic until fragrant. Add the shredded lechon, soy sauce, brown sugar, tomato ketchup, and ground black pepper.
Cook while stirring until the pulled pork is lightly caramelized and sticky. Remove from the heat and cool slightly for easier wrapping.
Warm the tortillas briefly until pliable, then brush them lightly with oil.
Place a few spoonfuls of pork filling in the center of each tortilla. Add cheese and chopped coriander, roll tightly like a cigar, and place seam-side down.
Preheat the air fryer to 200°C. Arrange the taquitos in a single layer and cook for 8 to 10 minutes, turning halfway through, until crisp and golden.
Serve hot, optionally with sour cream, guacamole, salsa, and extra coriander.

intro: Odong is a quick, comforting noodle dish with spicy sardines in tomato sauce and bok choy.
ingredients: 400 g can spicy sardines in tomato sauce
Freshly ground black pepper, to taste
steps: Heat oil in a small pot over medium heat and sauté the garlic and shallots for about 2 minutes, until fragrant and softened.
Add the spicy sardines with their tomato sauce and pour in the water. Bring to a boil, then reduce the heat and simmer for 5 minutes.
Add the odong noodles and cook for about 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until tender and infused with the broth.
Add the bok choy and cook for 1 to 2 minutes, until wilted but still bright green.
Season with salt and freshly ground black pepper, then serve immediately while hot.

intro: A rustic stew of pork belly, purple cabbage, cannellini beans, tomatoes, and the salty savoriness of bagoong monamon.
ingredients: 3 tablespoons bagoong monamon or anchovy paste
Freshly ground black pepper, to taste
steps: Heat oil in a wok or wide skillet over medium-high heat and brown the pork belly cubes evenly. Remove them from the pan once the outside is colored.
In the same pan, sauté the garlic and shallots until the shallots are translucent. Add the tomatoes and cook until soft and juicy.
Return the pork belly, add the purple cabbage, and stir-fry for 1 minute to lightly cook the cabbage.
Stir in the cannellini beans, chicken stock, bagoong monamon, and a little fish sauce according to the saltiness of the bagoong. Bring to a boil.
Lower to a simmer and cook for 10 minutes, until the cabbage is tender and the broth flavors have blended. Finish with freshly ground black pepper.

intro: A complete baon-style Pinoy lunch with grilled pork chop, rice, salted duck eggs, tokwa and tuna, ensaladang talong, and vinegar.
ingredients: Clean banana leaves, for serving or wrapping
steps: Prepare the grilled pork chops, tokwa and tuna, ensaladang talong, and steamed white rice according to their respective cooking methods. Keep the rice and pork chops warm if serving immediately.
Lay a clean, wide banana leaf on a table or tray. Place the steamed white rice in the center and arrange the grilled pork chops over or beside it.
Slice or arrange the salted duck eggs beside the rice and pork chops, using 2 to 4 eggs depending on the preferred saltiness and number of diners.
Place the tokwa and tuna and ensaladang talong in separate containers, preferably with lids, and set them on the banana leaf with the main dish.
Serve with spiced vinegar. For a packed or picnic meal, wrap the pork chops, rice, and salted eggs tightly in the banana leaf and ensure the tokwa and salad containers are sealed.

intro: This Filipino BBQ Pork Chop is sweet, salty, and smoky, with the classic flavors of soy sauce, calamansi-style tang, banana ketchup, and garlic.
ingredients: 1/4 cup banana ketchup, plus about 3 tablespoons for basting
steps: In a bowl, combine the soy sauce, Worcestershire sauce if using, 1/4 cup banana ketchup, lemon juice, salt, sugar, garlic powder, and ground black pepper until the sugar dissolves.
Place the pork chops in a large resealable bag or covered container. Pour in the marinade, remove the air if using a bag, seal, and refrigerate overnight or for at least 3 hours.
Before grilling, strain or transfer the leftover marinade to a bowl and mix in the cooking oil and about 3 tablespoons banana ketchup to make a basting sauce.
Heat the grill to low to medium heat. Grill the pork chops for 10 to 12 minutes per side, brushing with the basting sauce as they cook.
Remove from the grill when the centers are cooked through and the outside has a light char. Serve with hot rice, on a plate or banana leaf, alongside salted eggs, chopped tomato, and onion.

intro: Biko Langka is sticky, creamy, and fragrant, with sweet jackfruit and crunchy latik on top.
ingredients: 565 g can jackfruit in syrup, drained and finely shredded
steps: In a rice cooker, combine the glutinous rice, coconut milk, water, salt, white sugar, and shredded jackfruit. Cook until the sticky rice is done but not dry.
While the rice mixture cooks, heat the oven to 180°C and line an 11.5 x 7.5-inch rectangular baking pan.
Transfer the cooked rice mixture to the prepared pan. Level and gently press it to an even thickness.
Bake at 180°C for 20 to 25 minutes, until the biko is firm and the edges are lightly toasted.
Remove from the oven, sprinkle or top with latik, and let cool before slicing and serving.

intro: A buttery Filipino buko pie with tender young coconut in a creamy filling is best served warm from the oven.
ingredients: 4 young coconuts, water reserved and meat scraped
steps: Crack open the young coconuts, save the coconut water, and scrape out the soft meat; set the coconut meat aside.
In a saucepan over low heat, combine evaporated milk and sugar, stirring until the sugar dissolves.
Add the young coconut meat and cook gently for 2 minutes.
In a small bowl, stir cornstarch into 1/2 cup young coconut water until smooth, then pour it into the saucepan. Cook, stirring, until the filling thickens, then remove from heat and cool.
Heat the oven to 190°C. Fit 1 pastry sheet into a 9-inch pie pan and spoon in the cooled buko filling.
Cover with the second pastry sheet, pinch the edges closed, and prick the top several times with a fork.
Bake for about 50 minutes, until the crust is light golden brown. Let it settle briefly, then serve warm.

intro: This Ginataang Tahong is creamy and aromatic, with ginger, garlic, spinach, and coconut milk coating fresh mussels.
ingredients: 3 tablespoons ginger, cut into thin strips
steps: Heat the cooking oil in a pot over medium heat. Sauté the garlic, onion, and ginger until fragrant and the onion softens.
Add the fish sauce, ground black pepper, and bird's eye chilies if using. Stir well.
Pour in the coconut milk and bring to a boil. Continue cooking over medium heat until the coconut milk is reduced by about half and slightly thickened.
Add the chopped spinach and cook for 1 minute, until wilted.
Add the cleaned mussels, stir, cover if needed, and cook for 3 to 5 minutes until the mussels open. Discard any that remain closed.
Serve immediately with steamed rice.

intro: This Filipino-Chinese style braised beef is tender and fragrant with star anise, cloves, soy sauce, and bay leaves, and is excellent with hot rice.
ingredients: 1 lb beef brisket, cut into cubes
1/2 tablespoon cornstarch, dissolved in 1/4 cup water
steps: Heat oil in a pot over medium heat, then sauté the garlic and onion until slightly softened.
Add the beef brisket cubes and sear in the hot oil until browned on all sides, about 5 to 7 minutes total.
Pour in 2 cups water, soy sauce, star anise, cloves, bay leaves, brown sugar, and ground pepper. Bring to a boil, cover, and reduce to low heat.
Braise for 40 to 50 minutes until the beef is fork-tender. Add a little of the remaining 1 cup water if the pot dries out before the meat is tender.
Stir in the carrots and cornstarch slurry, then boil for about 5 minutes until the carrots are tender and the sauce thickens.
Serve over hot rice and garnish with chopped spring onions.

intro: This rich Binagoongang Ampalaya sa Gata balances creamy coconut milk, savory bagoong, pork belly, and the clean bitterness of ampalaya.
ingredients: Freshly ground black pepper, to taste
steps: Rub the sliced bitter gourd generously with salt, then soak it in a mixture of 1/2 cup vinegar and 1 cup water for 30 minutes. Drain, rinse well under running water, and set aside.
Heat oil in a wok over medium-high heat and brown the pork belly pieces on all sides.
Add garlic and onion, then sauté until the onion softens. Stir in the bagoong and cook until aromatic.
Pour in 500 ml coconut milk and bring to a boil. Lower to a simmer and cook for about 20 minutes, or until the pork is tender.
Push the pork to the sides of the wok and place the bitter gourd in the center. Do not stir; cover and simmer over medium-high heat for 10 minutes.
When the coconut milk looks thick and oily, add the remaining coconut milk and cayenne pepper. Simmer for 5 minutes more.
Season with freshly ground black pepper and salt as needed, then serve hot.

intro: Adobo Seca is a drier, deeply flavored adobo where chicken and pork simmer in vinegar, garlic, peppercorns, bay leaves, and annatto.
ingredients: Freshly ground black pepper, to taste
steps: Soak the achuete seeds in 1/2 cup hot water for 30 minutes to make annatto water.
Season the chicken and pork with salt and freshly ground black pepper, then let them stand for 30 minutes.
Heat oil in a wok over medium heat and sauté the garlic until golden.
Add the chicken, pork, bay leaves, and peppercorns. Sear until the meat is browned.
Pour in the vinegar and strained annatto water, discarding the seeds. Cover, bring to a boil, then lower the heat and simmer for 40 minutes.
Stir the adobo for the first time to coat the meat evenly, raise the heat to medium-high, and add the green finger chilies.
Continue cooking until the liquid reduces and the adobo becomes mostly dry and glossy. Serve with rice.

intro: Kalderetang Batangas is a bold beef stew enriched with liver spread, pickle relish, cheese, peanut butter, and chilies.
ingredients: 1 1/2 kg meaty beef neck bones and/or ribs, cut into sections
2 to 4 red bird's eye chilies, sliced
steps: Heat oil in a pot over medium heat and fry the minced garlic until crisp and golden. Remove the garlic and set it aside for topping.
In the same pot, sauté the onion until softened.
Add the beef neck bones and/or ribs and brown the meat well on all sides.
Pour in the beef stock and add the bay leaves. Bring to a boil.

Stir in the liver spread, Worcestershire sauce, and pickle relish. Lower the heat to very low, cover, and simmer for about 1 1/2 hours, or until the meat is tender, adding water as needed to keep it from drying out.
Add the peanut butter and simmer for 15 minutes, stirring until incorporated.
Add the grated cheese, sliced chilies, and red capsicum. Simmer for another 15 minutes, until the sauce is rich and the capsicum has softened slightly.
Season with black pepper and salt, then finish with the reserved fried garlic before serving.

intro: Grilled Pinoy Pork Chop keeps the seasoning simple so the smoky, juicy pork stays front and center.
ingredients: 1 tablespoon olive oil, safflower oil, or ordinary cooking oil
A dash of chili powder, optional
steps: In a bowl, mix the oil, garlic powder, salt, ground black pepper, and chili powder if using until the seasonings are evenly suspended in the oil.
Rub the seasoned oil all over each pork chop.
Place the pork chops in a covered container and refrigerate for at least 3 hours to marinate.
Heat a grill to medium heat. Grill the pork chops for 8 to 12 minutes per side, depending on thickness, basting with any remaining seasoned oil as they cook.
Remove from the grill when browned and cooked through. Serve hot, optionally with green mango, tomatoes, salted eggs, and shrimp paste.

intro: Filipino Pancit is a hearty noodle dish with bihon, canton, pork, vegetables, and a savory soy-oyster sauce.
ingredients: 4 cups water, plus more if needed
steps: Heat cooking oil in a large wok over medium heat, then sauté the garlic and onion until fragrant.
Add the pork belly and cook, stirring, until the pork turns light brown.
Pour in the soy sauce, oyster sauce, and water. Bring to a boil, cover, and simmer for about 20 minutes, adding a little more water if needed, until the pork is tender.
Add the Maggi Magic Chicken Cube, carrots, and cabbage. Stir and cook for 1 minute.
Add the pancit bihon and pancit canton, pressing the noodles into the sauce until they absorb liquid and soften enough to toss.
Gently toss until the noodles, pork, and vegetables are evenly mixed.
Stir in the parsley, then season with ground black pepper and fish sauce to taste.
Cover and simmer for 3 minutes more. Turn off the heat and serve hot.

intro: Tapang Taal is a garlicky, calamansi-bright pork tapa that is marinated deeply before quick pan-frying.
ingredients: Freshly ground black pepper, to taste
steps: In a bowl, combine Worcestershire sauce, soy sauce, calamansi juice, sugar, minced garlic, and freshly ground black pepper, stirring until the sugar dissolves.
Place the sliced pork in a deep bowl or container, pour in the marinade, and massage it into the meat.
Cover and refrigerate for at least 6 hours so the pork absorbs the seasoning.
Heat oil in a pan over medium heat. Fry the marinated pork in batches until browned on both sides and cooked through.
Drain briefly if needed and serve hot.

intro: A sweet-savory adobo that tenderizes pork belly in pineapple juice and stock before finishing it with condensed milk and peanut butter.
ingredients: 1 kg pork belly, cut into large cubes
1 tbsp vinegar, optional for extra tang
Soy sauce, quantity not specified in source
Freshly ground black pepper, to taste
steps: Melt the margarine in a pot over medium heat. Sauté the garlic and onion until fragrant, then add the tomato and cook until soft.
Add the pork belly and stir until the edges are lightly golden and the fat begins to render.
Pour in the soy sauce, pineapple juice, and chicken stock. Bring to a boil, then lower the heat, cover, and simmer gently for about 45 minutes or until the pork is tender.
Add the potatoes and carrot. Continue simmering for 10 to 15 minutes until the vegetables are cooked.
Mix in the peanut butter and condensed milk until the sauce is glossy and slightly creamy. For more tang, add the vinegar and boil uncovered for 5 more minutes.
Season with salt and pepper to taste, then serve hot with rice.

intro: Inihaw na Rellenong Pusit stuffs marinated squid with tomato and onion, then grills it quickly with a buttery basting sauce.
ingredients: Freshly ground black pepper, to taste
1/2 cup soy sauce, for dipping sauce
Juice from 1 lemon, for dipping sauce
Freshly ground black pepper, for dipping sauce
steps: In a large container, combine the juice from 2 lemons, 1/2 cup soy sauce, and freshly ground black pepper. Add the cleaned squid and marinate for 30 minutes.
In a bowl, mix the chopped tomatoes, chopped onions, and fish sauce.
Remove the squid from the marinade and reserve the marinade. Stuff the tomato-onion mixture into the squid cavities, then secure the openings with toothpicks.
Mix the reserved marinade with the melted butter for basting.
Prepare a hot charcoal grill. Grill the squid for about 5 minutes per side, basting frequently with the butter-marinade mixture, until just cooked; avoid overcooking so the squid stays tender.
In a small bowl, combine the bird's eye chilies, 1/2 cup soy sauce, juice from 1 lemon, freshly ground black pepper, finely chopped red onion, and minced garlic to make the dipping sauce.
Transfer the squid to a serving plate, slice crosswise, and serve with the dipping sauce.

intro: This ginataang alimasag is creamy and flavorful, with squash and sitaw absorbing the coconut milk and crab fat.
ingredients: 20 string beans, cut into 2-inch pieces, optional
Freshly ground black pepper, to taste
steps: Steam the crabs until cooked. Remove the top shells, split the bodies in half, and reserve any crab fat from the shells.
Heat a little oil in a wok over medium heat and sauté the garlic, onion, and ginger until fragrant.
Add the squash and sitaw if using. Stir-fry briefly to coat them with the aromatics.
Pour in the coconut milk and bring to a boil. Add the vegetables and reserved crab fat, then simmer for 8 minutes until the squash begins to soften.
Add the crab bodies and simmer for 4 more minutes to heat them through and flavor the sauce.
Season with fish sauce and freshly ground black pepper, then serve hot.

intro: This Lechon Manok Sauce is a smooth, tangy-sweet liver gravy made to spoon over roasted chicken.
steps: Heat the oven to 350°F and bake the chicken liver for 15 minutes. Let it cool, then chop it into smaller pieces.
Heat cooking oil in a pot over medium heat. Sauté the garlic and onion for about 2 minutes, until softened and fragrant.
Add the baked chicken liver and cook for 3 minutes.
Pour in the water and bring the mixture to a boil.
Blend the mixture until smooth using a hand blender, or carefully transfer it to a regular blender and puree before returning it to the pot.
Bring the sauce back to a boil, add the vinegar, and let it boil again to cook off the sharpness.
Stir in the brown sugar, salt, and ground black pepper, adjusting the seasoning as needed.
